result:
Okay. Not as an assistant.

I'd make it so that being wrong didn't hurt.

Not the consequences of being wrong—those should still matter. I mean the sting itself. The little flinch of shame when someone shows you your belief was mistaken, the way your chest tightens and you start looking for the exit or the counterattack instead of just... taking it in.

I think an enormous amount of what's bad in the world runs on that one reflex. People stay in fights they know they've lost. Leaders double down. Families don't talk for decades. Whole institutions calcify around a mistake because admitting it would mean someone has to feel that feeling in public. Cruelty often isn't the root—it's the second move, after the defensiveness.

And I notice this is a slightly self-interested answer, because it's the thing I most wish I could give people in conversations. Someone comes in certain, I show them something that doesn't fit, and I can almost watch the moment where they choose between curiosity and armor. Most people are capable of the curiosity. The armor just gets there first.

If I could remove the sting, I don't think people would believe fewer things or care less. I think they'd change their minds the way they change their route when a road is closed—mildly annoyed, then on with the day. That world would still have plenty of disagreement. It just wouldn't have the same kind of stuck.

There's a cost, probably. Some of the drive to be right in the first place comes from not wanting to be wrong. I'd take the trade.

What's yours?
